plan.title: Weather: Air, Clouds & Fronts
plan.hook: Read the sky as moving air and changing water, then separate what a forecast predicts from what it can promise.
objectives: Explain the pressure-gradient contribution to wind.
Connect rising air, cooling and cloud formation.
Interpret fronts without treating them as guaranteed storms.

sections.heading: Uneven heating starts a circulation
sections.body:
Sunlight heats Earth unevenly. Surface type, latitude, season and time of day affect energy absorption. These differences help establish temperature and pressure patterns. A pressure-gradient force pushes air toward lower pressure.

Wind does not necessarily blow straight from a high-pressure centre to a low-pressure centre. Earth's rotation deflects moving air relative to the ground, and surface friction also changes its motion. The actual wind reflects these combined influences. Closely spaced pressure contours usually indicate a stronger pressure gradient, though terrain and height matter too.

A daytime sea breeze illustrates a local circulation. Land often warms faster than nearby water, helping establish a flow with cooler marine air moving inland near the surface and return flow aloft. The broader weather pattern can strengthen, alter or overwhelm it. A sea breeze is a useful model, not a guaranteed event at every coast each afternoon.
sections.visual: In this daytime sea-breeze model, warmer land helps air rise. Cooler air moves inland at the surface, and air returns toward the sea aloft. Real winds also depend on rotation, friction and larger weather systems.

questions.q: Why is “wind always moves directly from high to low pressure” incomplete?
questions.hint: Name the influences besides the pressure gradient.
questions.answer: Rotation and friction also affect moving air, so the wind need not point directly along the pressure-gradient force.

sections.heading: Rising air can make water visible
sections.body:
Water vapour is an invisible gas. A cloud contains tiny suspended liquid droplets, ice crystals, or both. Cloud visibility is therefore different from the mere presence of water vapour in air.

An air parcel rising into lower surrounding pressure expands. Without enough heat added to compensate, expansion cools it. If it cools to saturation, water can condense onto small airborne particles. Condensation releases latent heat, so saturated rising air cools differently from unsaturated air.

Relative humidity compares actual water-vapour pressure with saturation vapour pressure at the same temperature. Cooling can increase relative humidity without adding water: the saturation value decreases. A parcel can reach saturation near its dew point with unchanged initial moisture content.

Cloud formation does not guarantee rain at the ground. Droplets or crystals must grow enough to fall, and precipitation can evaporate in dry air below. Lifting, moisture and the vertical temperature profile all matter.
sections.visual: As a parcel rises into lower pressure, it expands and cools. If it reaches saturation, water vapour can condense into cloud droplets. Falling precipitation can evaporate in drier air below the cloud.

questions.q: Can relative humidity rise without water being added?
questions.hint: Change temperature instead of moisture supply.
questions.answer: Yes. Cooling lowers saturation vapour pressure, so the same initial vapour amount represents a larger fraction of saturation.

sections.heading: A front supplies one ingredient
sections.body:
A front is a boundary between air masses with different properties, especially temperature and density. Advancing colder air at a cold front can lift warmer air. At a warm front, warmer air advances over a retreating cooler air mass. Boundary slope, moisture and stability affect the cloud and precipitation pattern.

“Cold front means thunderstorm” is an unreliable shortcut. A front can provide lifting, but deep storms also need suitable moisture and instability. Another cold front may bring mainly a wind shift and temperature change.

Forecasts estimate atmospheric evolution from imperfect observations and models. Uncertainty can grow, producing different plausible timings, locations and intensities. Comparing a range of outcomes helps describe that uncertainty rather than pretending it is absent. For an actual outdoor decision, match the forecast to your location and time window and follow current official local alerts for severe weather.
sections.visual: At a simplified cold front, denser advancing air wedges beneath warmer air and forces it upward. Moisture and atmospheric stability help determine whether this lift produces cloud, rain or thunderstorms.

questions.q: Why can two cold fronts bring very different weather?
questions.answer: Their moisture, stability and lifting strength can differ. The same boundary category does not guarantee the same cloud or storm development.

questions.q: Which way does the pressure-gradient force point?
questions.explain: The force points toward lower pressure. The resulting wind also depends on rotation, friction and the flow history.

questions.q: Why might a sea breeze not develop on a particular afternoon?
choices: A stronger background weather pattern can overwhelm the local circulation
questions.explain: The local heating contrast interacts with the larger pressure and wind pattern. It does not guarantee a daily circulation by itself.

questions.q: What makes an ordinary cloud visible?
questions.explain: The visible particles scatter light. Water vapour itself is invisible.

questions.q: Unsaturated air cools with initially unchanged water-vapour content. What generally happens?
choices: Rain must immediately reach the ground
questions.explain: Saturation vapour pressure decreases with cooling, raising relative humidity. Surface rain still requires further processes.

questions.q: Which statement about cold fronts is most reliable?
choices: They can lift warmer air, with outcomes depending on other conditions
questions.explain: Cold fronts can supply lifting, but storm development also depends on moisture and instability.

questions.q: What does comparing plausible forecast outcomes help you assess?
choices: A guarantee that every model is correct
Uncertainty in timing, location and intensity
Whether old lessons replace current alerts
questions.explain: A range of predictions reveals uncertainty. It does not remove the need for updated observations and official alerts.
